review.title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes
review.summary: The paper introduces Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes (SGVB), a reparameterization of the variational lower bound that yields a differentiable unbiased estimator optimizable with stochastic gradients. For i.i.d. datasets with continuous latent variables per datapoint, they propose Auto-Encoding VB (AEVB), which learns a recognition model (encoder) to amortize inference cost, enabling efficient joint learning of generative and variational parameters. The method is demonstrated on MNIST and Frey Face datasets using a variational auto-encoder with a Gaussian approximate posterior. Theoretical advantages are claimed to be reflected in experimental results showing faster convergence and higher lower bounds compared to the wake-sleep algorithm and Monte Carlo EM.

strengths.point: The reparameterization trick enables a low-variance, differentiable estimator of the variational lower bound, making stochastic gradient optimization feasible for models with intractable posteriors.
strengths.quote: We show how a reparameterization of the variational lower bound yields a simple differentiable unbiased estimator of the lower bound; this SGVB (Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes) estimator can be used for efficient approximate posterior inference in almost any model with continuous latent variables and/or parameters, and is straightforward to optimize using standard stochastic gradient ascent techniques.

strengths.point: The AEVB algorithm amortizes inference by learning a recognition model, avoiding per-datapoint iterative inference schemes like MCMC.
strengths.quote: In the AEVB algorithm we make inference and learning especially efficient by using the SGVB estimator to optimize a recognition model that allows us to perform very efficient approximate posterior inference using simple ancestral sampling, which in turn allows us to efficiently learn the model parameters, without the need of expensive iterative inference schemes (such as MCMC) per datapoint.

strengths.point: A concrete algorithm with pseudocode and a worked-out Gaussian example is provided, including minibatch settings and optimizer choice.
strengths.quote: Minibatch version of the Auto-Encoding VB (AEVB) algorithm. Either of the two SGVB estimators in section~\ref{subsec:our_estimator} can be used. We use settings $M=100$ and $L=1$ in experiments.

concerns.point: The paper states that the estimator variance is small (<1) and omits it, but provides no quantitative variance measurements, error bars, or repeated-run statistics to support this claim.
concerns.quote: The estimator variance was small ($<1$) and omitted.
concerns.suggestion: Report variance of the gradient estimator across multiple runs or minibatches; include error bars in figures and a table of final log-likelihood values with standard deviations.

concerns.point: The experimental comparison only includes wake-sleep and Monte Carlo EM; the wake-sleep algorithm is not described in the main text, and other relevant baselines (e.g., stochastic variational inference with control variates) are cited but not compared.
concerns.quote: We compared performance of AEVB to the wake-sleep algorithm~\cite{hinton1995wake}.
concerns.suggestion: Provide a clear description of the wake-sleep implementation used; add comparisons with at least one modern stochastic variational inference baseline (e.g., Hoffman et al. 2013 or Ranganath et al. 2013).

withdrawn.point: The manuscript contains extensive duplicated sections (Introduction, Method, Example, Related work, Experiments, Conclusion, Future work appear multiple times), indicating a serious preparation error that hinders readability and assessment.
withdrawn.why: Checked in the LaTeX source by code: no section heading and no paragraph appears twice.

withdrawn.point: The claim that wake-sleep is the only other on-line method for continuous latent variable models is incorrect; the paper itself cites Hoffman et al. (2013) on stochastic variational inference, which is also an on-line method for the same class.
withdrawn.why: The paper cites Hoffman et al. (2013) as stochastic variational inference with control variates, but does not present it as an on-line learning method for the same general class of continuous latent variable models; the referee's characterization is not in the text.

withdrawn.point: The reparameterization trick is presented as general but only the Gaussian diagonal-covariance case is worked out and tested; no experiments or details are given for other distributions listed (Laplace, Gamma, etc.).
withdrawn.why: The paper provides general reparameterization strategies and explicit distribution examples (including Laplace, Gamma, etc.) in the 'The reparameterization trick' section, so the claim that no details are given for other distributions is incorrect.

checklist.quote: We trained generative models of images from the MNIST and Frey Face datasets\footnote{Available at \url{http://www.cs.nyu.edu/~roweis/data.html}}
checklist.note: Datasets are public but preprocessing (e.g., binarization of MNIST) is not described.
No code availability statement or repository link is provided.

checklist.item: Method described fully enough to implement
checklist.note: Pseudocode and Gaussian estimator are given, but MLP architecture details (hidden layer size, activation) are only in the appendix.

checklist.quote: We use settings $M=100$ and $L=1$ in experiments. All parameters were updated using the Adagrad stepsizes (with accompanying annealing schedule).
checklist.note: Minibatch size, samples per datapoint, optimizer, and initialization (N(0,0.01)) are specified.
No mention of hardware, runtime, or software framework.
No random seeds, number of repetitions, or averaging over runs are reported.

checklist.quote: The estimator variance was small ($<1$) and omitted.
checklist.note: Figures show single curves without error bars; no quantitative variability measures are provided.

checklist.quote: We compared performance of AEVB to the wake-sleep algorithm~\cite{hinton1995wake}.
checklist.note: Wake-sleep and Monte Carlo EM are compared, but wake-sleep is not fully described and other relevant baselines (e.g., stochastic VI with control variates) are omitted.
Variational lower bound and marginal log-likelihood are clearly defined.

checklist.quote: Since the SGVB estimator and the AEVB algorithm can be applied to almost any inference and learning problem with continuous latent variables, there are plenty of future directions...
checklist.note: The paper lists future work but does not explicitly discuss limitations of the proposed method (e.g., variance of estimator for small minibatches, restriction to continuous latents, diagonal covariance assumption).

questions: Why is wake-sleep described as the only on-line method when stochastic variational inference (Hoffman et al., 2013) is also an on-line method for continuous latent variables and is cited in the paper?
Can you provide quantitative results (final log-likelihood values, error bars over multiple random seeds) to substantiate the claimed faster convergence and higher bounds of AEVB?

Have you tested the reparameterization trick with non-Gaussian approximate posteriors (e.g., Laplace, Gamma) as suggested in the paper, or is the current implementation limited to the Gaussian diagonal-covariance case?

queries: amortized variational inference recognition model encoder

related.title: Learning Wake-Sleep Recurrent Attention Models
related.note: The references section cites 'Auto-encoding variational Bayes' (Kingma & Welling, 2014) alongside the wake-sleep algorithm, indicating the paper is a contemporary alternative to wake-sleep for amortized inference.

related.title: Reweighted Wake-Sleep
related.note: This work proposes 'Reweighted Wake-Sleep', a direct modification of the wake-sleep algorithm which the paper under review compares against experimentally.

related.title: From Amortised to Memoised Inference: Combining Wake ...
related.note: The 'Wake-Sleep-Remember' algorithm combines wake-sleep with memoization; since the paper under review benchmarks against wake-sleep, this later work extends the baseline the paper compares to.

related.title: Iterative Amortized Inference
related.note: Discusses 'Iterative Amortized Inference' and explicitly cites the variational auto-encoder (Kingma & Welling, 2014; Rezende et al., 2014) as the foundational method for amortizing inference via an encoder network.

related.title: Amortized Inference Regularization
related.note: Analyzes the regularization effects of the amortized inference model introduced by the variational autoencoder (Kingma & Welling, 2014), directly building on the AEVB framework proposed in the paper.

related.title: Instance-Adaptive Parametrization for Amortized Variational Inference
related.note: Proposes 'Instance-Adaptive Parametrization' to increase the flexibility of the amortized inference model (encoder) central to the AEVB/VAE architecture described in the paper.

related.title: Reducing Reparameterization Gradient Variance - cs.Princeton
related.note: Addresses variance reduction for reparameterization gradients in Gaussian Monte Carlo variational inference, directly relevant to the SGVB estimator and Gaussian approximate posterior used in the paper's AEVB experiments.

related.assessment: The paper introduces the foundational SGVB estimator and AEVB/VAE framework for amortized inference with continuous latent variables. The search results confirm its seminal status: later works explicitly cite it as the basis for the VAE architecture, analyze its regularization properties, extend its encoder flexibility, and modify the wake-sleep baseline it outperforms. The snippets do not reveal the specific SGVB reparameterization derivation or the exact experimental hyperparameters, so the novelty of the gradient estimator itself versus the VAE application cannot be fully disentangled from the snippets alone.

figures.1: This is a directed graphical model diagram (also called a Bayesian network or probabilistic graphical model). **Blocks/Nodes**: - A top node labeled "z" with a value "2". - A bottom node labeled "x" with a value "N". **Lines**: - Solid lines: One from "z" to "x" (labeled "θ"), and one from "θ" to "z" (labeled "θ"). - Dashed lines: One from "φ" to "z" (labeled "φ"), and one from "z" to "x" (dashed, part of the variational approximation). **Labels/Values**: - Nodes: "z" (value "2"), "x" (value "N"). - Parameters: "φ" (connected to "z"), "θ" (connected to both "z" and "x"). **Structure**: The diagram illustrates a generative model where "z" (latent variable, value 2) influences "x" (observed variable, value N). Solid lines represent the generative model \( p_\theta(z)p_\theta(x|z) \), and dashed lines represent the variational approximation \( q_\phi(z|x) \). Parameters \( \phi \) and \( \theta \) are learned jointly. **Figure Caption**: "Figure 1: The type of directed graphical model under consideration. Solid lines denote the generative model \( p_\theta(z)p_\theta(x|z) \), dashed lines denote the variational approximation \( q_\phi(z|x) \) to the intractable posterior \( p_\theta(z|x) \). The variational parameters \( \phi \) are learned jointly with the generative model pa- rameters \( \theta \)."
figures.2: This is a figure consisting of six line graphs arranged in two rows and three columns. Each graph compares the performance of two methods (Wake-Sleep and AEVB) on different datasets (MNIST and Frey Face) with varying latent space dimensions (Nz). ### Axes and Labels: - **X-axis**: All graphs share the same x-axis label: "# Training samples evaluated," with tick marks at 10⁵, 10⁶, 10⁷, and 10⁸. - **Y-axis**: - Top row (MNIST datasets): Labeled "L" with tick marks from -150 to -100 (left) and -150 to -100 (right). - Bottom row (Frey Face datasets): Labeled "L" with tick marks from 0 to 1600 (left) and 0 to 1600 (right). ### Panels (from left to right, top to bottom): 1. **MNIST, Nz=3**: - Y-axis: -150 to -100. - Legend: "Wake-Sleep (test)" (green dashed line), "Wake-Sleep (train)" (green solid line), "AEVB (test)" (red dashed line), "AEVB (train)" (red solid line). - Trend: All lines start near -150 at 10⁵ samples and rise toward -100 as samples increase. 2. **MNIST, Nz=5**: - Y-axis: -150 to -100. - Same legend and line styles as above. - Trend: Similar to Nz=3, lines rise from ~-150 to ~-100 with increasing samples. 3. **MNIST, Nz=10**: - Y-axis: -150 to -100. - Same legend and line styles. - Trend: Lines rise from ~-150 to ~-100 as samples increase.
figures.3: This is a scientific figure with two side-by-side line graphs (panels) comparing the estimated marginal log-likelihood of different algorithms as a function of training samples evaluated. ### Left Panel (N_train = 1000): - **X-axis**: "# Training samples evaluated (millions)" with tick marks at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. - **Y-axis**: "Marginal log-likelihood" with tick marks at -160, -150, -140, -130, -120, -110, -100, -100 (note: the top tick is labeled -100, but the axis extends to -160). - **Curves**: - Green solid line: "Wake-Sleep (train)" - Green dashed line: "Wake-Sleep (test)" - Blue dashed line: "MCEM (train)" - Blue dashed line with dots: "MCEM (test)" - Red solid line: "AEVB (train)" - Red dashed line: "AEVB (test)" - **Trend**: All curves start near -160 log-likelihood and rise sharply as training samples increase, with AEVB (train) and (test) reaching the highest values (around -100) first, followed by Wake-Sleep (train) and (test), then MCEM (train) and (test), which plateau lower (around -130 to -140). ### Right Panel (N_train = 50000): - **X-axis**: "# Training samples evaluated (millions)" with tick marks at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. - **Y-axis**: "Marginal log-likelihood" with tick marks at 160, 155, 150, 145, 140,
figures.4: This figure consists of two panels labeled (a) and (b), each showing a grid of images. ### Panel (a): Learned Frey Face manifold - **Content**: A 10x10 grid of grayscale facial images. Each row and column contains repeated faces with slight variations (e.g., different facial expressions or orientations). - **Labels**: Below the panel, the label reads "(a) Learned Frey Face manifold". ### Panel (b): Learned MNIST manifold - **Content**: A 10x10 grid of grayscale digit images (0-9). Each row and column shows digits with minor variations (e.g., different angles, slight distortions). - **Labels**: Below the panel, the label reads "(b) Learned MNIST manifold". ### Figure Caption (text below the panels): "Figure 4: Visualisations of learned data manifold for generative models with two-dimensional latent space, learned with AEVB. Since the prior of the latent space is Gaussian, linearly spaced coor- dinates on the unit square were transformed through the inverse CDF of the Gaussian to produce values of the latent variables z. For each of these values z, we plotted the corresponding generative pθ(x|z) with the learned parameters θ." ### Main Trend/Structure: Both panels visualize how a generative model (with a 2D latent space) interpolates between data points by varying the latent variables z. Each grid cell corresponds to a specific z value, and the images in each cell are the model’s output (pθ(x|z)) for that z. The structure shows continuous transitions between similar images (e.g., faces or digits) across adjacent grid cells, reflecting the learned manifold structure.
figures.5: This is a figure consisting of four panels arranged horizontally, each labeled with a letter and a description of the latent space dimensionality. The panels show rows of handwritten digits generated by different generative models, each corresponding to a different dimensionality of the latent space. - **Panel (a)**: Labeled "2-D latent space". It shows multiple rows of handwritten digits, with each row containing several digits. The digits are somewhat distorted but recognizable as numbers from 0 to 9. - **Panel (b)**: Labeled "5-D latent space". This panel also contains multiple rows of handwritten digits, similar in appearance to panel (a), but the digits may appear slightly more varied or less consistent than in panel (a). - **Panel (c)**: Labeled "10-D latent space". This panel shows rows of handwritten digits, which appear more varied and some digits may be less clear or more distorted compared to panels (a) and (b). - **Panel (d)**: Labeled "20-D latent space". This panel contains rows of handwritten digits, which appear more varied and less consistent in shape compared to the previous panels, with some digits being more distorted or less recognizable. Below the panels, there is a caption: "Figure 5: Random samples from learned generative models of MNIST for different dimensionalities of latent space."
